title: Contributing to a fork: two remotes, one branch
summary: The open-source workflow: your fork is `origin`, the project is `upstream`. Keep your fork current, base work on the project's latest, and never push to the wrong one.
mental_model: A remote is a named URL plus a set of tracking refs. Nothing stops you having several. The fork workflow is just the discipline of always fetching from `upstream` and always pushing to `origin`.

steps.title: Look at your two remotes
steps.why: `upstream` is the project you are contributing to; `origin` is your own fork, the only one you can push to. Naming them this way is a near-universal convention — follow it and every guide you read will make sense.
steps.expect: Two remotes. Your main tracks origin, not upstream.

steps.title: See how far behind the project you are
steps.why: The project moved twice since you forked. Fetching upstream updates `upstream/main` and nothing else — your branches and your fork are untouched.
steps.expect: Two commits you do not have.

verify.label: you can see exactly what upstream has added

steps.title: Bring your fork's main up to date
steps.why: Fast-forward your local main to upstream's, then push it to your fork. Your fork's main should always be a mirror of the project — never a place you commit to directly.
steps.expect: A fast-forward, then your fork matches the project.

steps.title: Branch your contribution from the project's latest
steps.why: Branching from up-to-date main means your pull request will apply cleanly. Branching from a stale fork is the single most common reason a first contribution needs a rebase before review.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Add a version parsing helper"

verify.label: your branch is exactly one commit ahead of upstream
verify.hint: branch from upstream/main, not from a stale local main

steps.title: Push it to your fork, not the project
steps.why: You have no write access to upstream — the pull request is opened from your fork's branch. `push -u origin` records that pairing so future pushes go to the right place automatically.

verify.label: the contribution branch tracks your fork, not upstream

steps.title: Upstream moves again while you wait for review
steps.why: This is normal on any active project. Fetch and rebase your one commit onto their new tip; the pull request updates itself and stays a clean one-commit diff.
steps.expect: A conflict on core.py, because upstream changed the same line you built on.

steps.title: Resolve and republish
steps.why: Keep upstream's version number and your helper. Then force-push to your own fork — safe here because the branch is yours alone, which is exactly when forcing is acceptable.

verify.label: still a single clean commit on top of the latest upstream
your contribution is one commit on top of the current upstream
verify.hint: fetch upstream, then git rebase upstream/main

verify.label: the rebase kept upstream's change and yours
verify.hint: resolve in favour of upstream's version number, keep your helper

verify.label: the branch pushes to your fork, never to upstream

pitfalls: Committing directly on your fork's main makes every future sync a merge instead of a fast-forward. Keep main a pure mirror.
`git pull` on a fork pulls from origin — your fork — which is almost never what you want. Fetch upstream explicitly.
Force-pushing your own pull-request branch is fine and normal. Force-pushing anything on upstream is not, and you usually cannot anyway.
GitHub's 'Sync fork' button does the fast-forward for you, but only for the default branch.
cheatsheet: update your view of the project
sync your main, refusing to create a merge
